newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower, strong home sales cited.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower, strong home sales cited.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market erased an early advance and finished lower on Monday after the government reported an unexpected jump in August home sales.
The 6-3/4 percent bellwether 30-year Treasury bond ended at 97-26/32, down 7/32, to yield 6.92 percent, versus 6.91 percent at Friday's close.

The market took news of a 0.6 percent rise in August personal income and a like-sized gain in personal spending in stride. The gains matched economists' forecasts and represented a mild rebound from very subdued July levels.
But August home sales took the market aback. Consistently strong, home sales were expected to back down from the high number of July transactions.
Instead, the July figures were revised upward to an annualized rate of 795,000 and August home sales rose 4.7 percent to an annualized rate of 832,000.

"New home sales show amazing resilience," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. For months, economists have been ready to see signs of weakness in the interest-rate sensitive housing sector -- but to no avail.
Another piece of data that troubled the inflation-wary bond market was the so-called "prices paid" index of the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index (PMI).

The Chicago purchasers reported that its index slipped to 56.3 in September from what one economist termed a "torrid" reading of 60.0 in August. That slip was expected. But the bond market was less than enamored of a sharp rise in the September prices paid index to 59.3 from 51.8 in August.
"The numbers we got today, though not of first-tier importance, were enough to create selling pressure on the day," said Flanagan.
After the market reversed its advance and entered negative territory in mid-morning trade, it stayed in the minus column, moving in a very narrow range, for the rest of the session.
The Treasury sold $26.0 billion in three- and six-month bills at average yields of 5.01 percent and 5.17 percent, respectively.
"It was very quiet," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at CS First Boston, describing the afternoon session.
Dimick said the market was unlikely to "gap" higher until it gets "permission" from the NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) index if NAPM comes in around 52.0.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that the September NAPM index would read 52.5, barely changed from 52.6 August reading.
The NAPM index is due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT on Tuesday.
Dimick said if NAPM comes in at 52, that would serve as permission for the market to rally a little bit more.
He said the two-year note yield could move to 6.0 percent and the long bond yield to 6.84 percent.
"I think there's a chance for us to run back toward those limits before the payroll number rolls around," said Dimick, referring to the U.S. employment report due on Friday.
At the close, three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.04 percent. Six-month bill rates were up two basis points to 5.25 percent. Year bill rates rose three basis points to 5.69 percent.

Prices of the two-year notes slipped 2/32 to 99-26/32, yielding 6.10 percent. Five-year notes slipped 4/32 to 99-20/32, yielding 6.46 percent, and the 10-year note fell 5/32 to 101-6/32 to yield 6.70 percent.
